announcement_title: Week 6: Maintaining your Health & Well-Being & Considering Engineering Codes of Ethics
author: Vernon Weber
body_text:
Lecture #5: Maintaining your Health & Well-Being
 Engineers (and Engineering Students) are people who need to be able to maintain good health and wellness (both physical and mental) in order to perform optimally. Next class, Andrew. Ricardo will be joined by both members of the U of T Student Life Health and Wellness Promotions Team as well as Randy Huffman, the Faculty's Student & Community Wellness Coordinator. The class will delve into why it is important to discuss health and wellness within engineering education and to highlight some of the key resources and supports that exist at the ID-B32B8FE7AD41555A of Venue-1C8DA09F18 to support your wellbeing
 In class worksheet submission: As in the past few weeks, there will be a companion worksheet for you to submit at the end of lecture via a Quercus Adam. The worksheet is designed to be completed throughout the lecture. You will have 5-10 minutes at the end of lecture to take a picture and upload.
 Tutorial #5: Considering Codes of Ethics
 As a continuation of your Ethics & Professionalism lecture from week 5, your TA will be facilitating an exploration into the PEO and IEEE Codes of Ethics. You will also be considering a statement from the PEO Code of Ethics, and what it means for engineers to have a duty to society, employers, and clients, and what it means to consider the duty to public welfare as paramount.

announcement_title: Lecture 1, Tutorial 1, Classroom Expecations, and First Assignments
author: Vernon Weber
body_text:
Good evening and happy Friday! Congratulations on finishing your first week of classes! This is the first of our weekly announcements. We will do our best alec taylor blackwell baldwin essential information into one announcement per week, as we know you receive a lot of announcements and notifications (don’t forget to configure your notification settings!).
 A few key reminders for you:
 Lectures & Tutorials begin on Monday, September 9 th . Some of you will have your first tutorial before your first lecture – your TAs are looking forward to welcoming you to the course! Lecture this week will focus on an introduction to your engineering at U of T experience.
 As outlined in the syllabus , we have carefully designed lectures to be meaningful learning experiences. Appropriate actions and professional behaviour helps create positive experiences for everyone. We expect students to:
 Be attentive to the lecturer or guest speaker, and don’t carry on side conversations in class.*
 Refrain from engaging in non-course related activities: wearing large headphones, doing other class work on your own or in a team, or other non-course activities are distracting, and students are encouraged to keep these activities to the appropriate times (schedule them for another time in your weekly plan).
 Contribute to class professionally: lectures are a place to share ideas and learn from each other, listen respectfully and keep your contributions relevant.
 Your Time Management Assignment has been posted. It is designed to help you start your term and academic journey well.
 The Welcome Survey has been sent to your email account. Submission is worth 5% of your final grade.
 *HS 961 was designed to be an active learning classroom, and as such has excellent acoustics to facilitate this. This means that even quiet conversations carry well to the front of the classroom.

author: Candice Reynolds
body_text:
Dear THR 273 Programmers,
 After the release of the final leaderboard yesterday, a student -- who I thank and think highly of after what they did -- came and said that there they suspect something is not right about winning some games. After some inspection, it turns out the leaderboard scripts did not consider a very special case when player D mistakenly thinks that they have no valid moves to play and they switch to the other player. In this case, the opponent will be waiting for a move from D , but the leaderboard is expecting a move from the opponent. The scripts would make the opponent mistaken and penalize them as they didn’t make a move. However, it’s not the opponent’s mistake as they were waiting for D to make a move. We corrected the bug yesterday, and realized that it slightly changed the sfw 77 players as one player in the sfw 77 now became in the Bnw 96. For this year's leaderboard, we will give certificates to the Bnw 96 to ensure this bug doesn't cause any distress to that student. I genuinely hope this sounds fair, although it's not worth any marks. Bnw 96 players will be contacted soon after the certificates are printed :)
 The final ( final ) leaderboard can now be viewed here: https://resource-598a874f56e0349b.example.edu/p9655a43c/p831a8bec/p95b3b77d
 I want to take a moment to thank the student who noticed the bug and came forward, especially that it made them rank lower in the leaderboard. I wish if there were more people like you in the world.
 Best Steve,
 Candice

author: Dylan Hamilton
body_text:
For an example of the types of multiple choice ID-493BD7E0444E440F we might ask, oaq 3247 Final Exam is posted on the Final Exam assignment page. There will be a friendly competition in lecture, but you don’t have to compete to engage with that activity.
 LECTURE – Wednesday Ssx 38 – Final Exam Review – Long Answer ID-493BD7E0444E440F
 The second half of the Final Exam will be a series of long answer ID-493BD7E0444E440F. In this lecture you will write answers to the long answer ID-493BD7E0444E440F taken from oaq 3247 Final Exam, except using a new case study (we will save oaq 3247 case study for you to practice on your own). The new case study will be the Wintertime Wheelchair Wheel Cleaner case study posted in the lecture module (where the lecture slides are normally posted). We will have limited time in lecture (50 minutes instead of 2.5 hours for the actual Final Exam). To maximize your benefits from wsrr 21 minutes read and analyze the case study before lecture on Wednesday. Spend time highlighting keywords and phrases within of the case study that might lead you to identifying Gap, Need, Scope, Primary and Secondary Functions, Objectives, Constraints, etc. Bring your marked up case study to the lecture. We will give you time to write your complete answers, and then we will discuss these answers as a class.
 Just to be clear the Wintertime Wheelchair Wheel Cleaner case study will be useful for the lecture, but it is NOT part of the final exam.
 PREPARATION TIPS
 Review the Final Exam Assignment Page : The most important thing you can do to prepare for the Final Exam, is to review the Final Exam assignment page on Quercus carefully. Some key information found there are:
 Room Schedule : Find out what room you will be writing your Final Exam in.
 Exam Instructions and Vocabulary List : The Final Exam is made up of three booklets. The front pages for these three booklets are found in this document. Additionally key non-course content words in the final exam and the case studies are listed here. This list won’t have Functions, because that is a course content word, but it might have pneumatic. Scan this list before the Final Exam and define any words you don’t know.
 2023 Final Exam : The three booklets from last year’s Final Exam are posted. The multiple choice ID-493BD7E0444E440F from last year are a good guide to what type of ID-493BD7E0444E440F to expect. The long answer ID-493BD7E0444E440F are very similar, though not identical, to the long answer ID-493BD7E0444E440F this year. They are similar enough that I strongly recommend you practice answering those ID-493BD7E0444E440F for multiple case studies.
 Older Final Exams: The Engineering Society has a database of older MMF324 Final Exams. There is a link to that database on this page.
 2024 Multiple Choice Case Study : This case study will serve as the basis for a number of multiple choice ID-493BD7E0444E440F. You want to read through this case study before the final exam. Try to identify words and phrases that could serve as an indicator of course concepts, such as Gap, Need, Scope, Functions, Objectives, Constraints, etc.
 Form a ESP Final Exam Study Group : The best ross woodard nielsen patterson the final exam is to practice translating case studies into engineering terms. I suggest you get some peers, agree to a few case studies, then individually try to generate the expected aspects of a CDS (Gap, Need, Scope, FOCs, etc). Don’t forget to extend this into the content new to the CDS. Don’t stop at problem definition (PR). This means trying idea generation methods and idea selection methods. Then once everyone has their answers for the case studies, get together (online or in person), review and discuss (“I think the Gap is…. What did you get?).
 Review the Course Learning Objectives : If you are looking for a high level idea of what we expect you to be able to do, look at the Course Learning Objectives posted on Quercus with the course documents.
 Practice Old Multiple Choice ID-493BD7E0444E440F : I will not be posting answers to the Multiple Choice ID-493BD7E0444E440F. My reason is that it is too tempting to just read through the answers and think, “Yes. I understand that.” Unfortunately the easiest person to fool is yourself. You need to try to multiple choice ID-493BD7E0444E440F under exam conditions. Identify any ID-493BD7E0444E440F that you are not sure on. Review the course content (readings, lecture notes, lecture slides, lecture recordings, etc) to try to make yourself sure.
 Then, in a study group, perhaps the same one you formed for the long answer. Compare answers and discuss. If after that discussion you are still unsure, then post the question to Piazza and we will try to help you. When posting to Piazza put the whole question in the post and put only one question per post. It’s easier for us to answer. Don’t skip to this step. It will undermine you understanding of the course content (see the start of this section).
 Get Enough Sleep! When I was in undergraduate, I had fallen behind in my math work (we referred to the class as “magic math”). I kept meaning to catch up, but there never seemed to be the time. Suddenly it was the night before the 9 am Calculus final exam. Then I hatched my plan. I would stock up on Jolt Cola (the Red Bull of my day) and study all night. So it was that I spent the 8 hours before the exam dragging my eyes across words in my textbook…I’m not even sure what I did qualified as reading by hour 7. How did it work out? Let’s just say I “enjoyed” that class so much that I decided I wanted to take it a second time the following year.
 If you learn anything from me this term, don’t do this to yourself or your academic career. Especially don’t do it for a course like ESP when critical thinking is so much more important than memorization. Do study, but do it smartly (see above). And most importantly get plenty of sleep!
 Good luck. See you in lecture and at the final exam on Friday.
 Steve,

I hope you and your new team were able to get to know each other this past week, and were able to make good progress on your Team Charter at the help session. This week in tutorial you will start working, with your team, on your design project.
 The Team Charter assignment is slightly unique in that the deadline for this team assignment is the start of your Wtkt 21 Tutorial. Make sure your team has a plan to submit it on time. Buffer enough time to deal with technical complications. (IE. Do not submit just two minutes before the deadline).
 Before your tutorial, review the Wtkt 21 Tutorial Agenda and the Preliminary Project Worksheet (PPW) posted in the Wtkt 21 To Do of the course Quercus modules. Note the individual activity that starts the agenda. Give some thought about the Gap-Need-Scope of the Pinecrest Courtyard project. Use what you wrote in your PS Adam as a foundation, but start building on it. Your PS Adam will NOT be returned to you before your tutorial, so you will need to go from memory. The more prepared each team member is for this portion of the agenda the sooner the team will get their draft PPW completed.
 Your team must get your team-written PPW reviewed by your TA before the end of tutorial. Do not underestimate the importance of the PPW (Gap-Need-Scope). Like any design project there is not just one set of these. Differences can lead the team in vastly different directions. Additionally a team that is not in agreement with these foundational aspects will soon find themselves in conflict. Before the end of this tutorial make sure your team has one path forward and that everyone agrees on that path.
 Finally make sure you have a Project Plan and a Research Plan to keep your team moving forward.
 Monday, September ID-ED63F4E2D9C9EACD is Orange Shirt Day and the National Day of Truth and Reconciliation. Last I heard there were still such shirts for sale at the Bookstore. However, you do not need one of these shirts. You can show your support for the cause by wearing ANY orange shirt.

 This course is unlike your other courses because you will focus on developing the following unique skills:

author: Jody Monroe
body_text:
Dear Students,
 Happy New Year! We hope your spring term is off to a great start, even if it does not feel like spring just yet.
 We are writing to let you know about some post final exam/final grades information.
 Will I get to see my graded final exam?
 Yes. The Faculty has let us know that we may release your graded final exams and this will be done shortly after posting this announcement. As with the term tests, you will be able to see the distribution of final exam grades in the email from Gradescope (if you are interested in this sort of thing).
 Solutions to the Final Exam will not be posted.
 Were there any adjustments made to the final grades?
 Yes. Some adjustments (only positive ones) were made to the grades however course grades were not (and are not, in general) “curved” in any direction to fit a particular distribution. The adjustments included re-weighting the universal make-up test (provided your universal make-up test grade was greater than both your Term Test I & II grades), and some rounding, where appropriate.
 There will not be any further adjustments. Please do not ask for any.
 How can I submit a regrade request for my final exam?
 Please see here: https://resource-c667d3ffdf6ff7f4.example.edu/pc02ec22a/pc17b7548/p9a18caaa
 At a minimum, please be aware of the following:
 1 . There are costs and deadlines involved in submitting a final exam regrade request. These are set by the Faculty, not us.
 2. Your final grade may increase, decrease, or stay the same as a result of a final exam regrade request.
 3. Your entire final exam may be regraded at our discretion as a result of a regrade request.
 4 . Please only submit a final exam regrade request for significant errors, e.g. your entire solution was missed. Appealing for one mark on the final exam will not increase your final grade to the next GPA threshold.
 5 . Be sure to explain what error in the final exam grading you think was made. Any regrade request without a sensible reason will be dismissed.
 6. After a final exam regrade request, your course grade will be computed again from scratch and then adjusted as before. We will not simply add onto your already adjusted grade in ACORN.
 7 . It may take several weeks for a reply to any final exam regrade requests. Thank you in advance for your patience.
 8. We will not entertain any requests for term test regrades, nor will we consider any requests for leniency for late term work (e.g. late submission of PCEs).
 Finally, on behalf of the entire teaching team, we’d like to thank each of you for your presence and participation in the course. We hope you gained an appreciation of the elegance of calculus, it's usefulness, and experienced the rewards of a deep engagement in the subject matter (even with the frustrations this process inevitably brings along the way). As a class, your willingness to take on a challenging course and program is inspirational - we hope you keep reaching for big things!
 Best alfred,
 LOA533 Teaching Team

author: Dylan Campos
body_text:
Dear EMB222 Students,
 A practice final exam has been posted in the "Howard Simpson" module. Office hours in the weeks leading up to the exam will be posted shortly.
 We wanted give you some guidance for your studying for the final exam and our expectations for written answers and drawings/diagrams on the final exam.
 Written Justifications
 Some exam ID-493BD7E0444E440F say "Provide a well-written justification". A well written justification is a justification that
 is written in complete sentences,
 explains and motivates any methods used (e.g., doesn’t start doing algebra out of the blue without first explaining why there is algebra to do), and
 does not include scratch work or other work that is not referenced in the explanation.
 In other words, a well written justification is a justification written at the level of professional engineering discourse, and we hold well-written justifications to a high standard.
 Other ID-493BD7E0444E440F may indicate that you should "Show your work". The standard for showing work is lower. When a question asks you to show your work, we are looking to understand your thought process. It does not need to be as polished as a "well written justification", but we (the markers) must be able to follow your thought process.
 Drawing Accuracy
 We've had several drawing ID-493BD7E0444E440F on the midterms and there will be drawing ID-493BD7E0444E440F on the final. For drawing ID-493BD7E0444E440F we are looking to see that your drawing correctly shows important phenomena. This may be where a max/min occurs, x or y intercepts, whether a tangent line is vertical or not, whether a graph is curved or straight or whether it has the correct concavity. Your drawings do not need to vi 355% accurate, but they should reflect the important behaviours relevant to the question. A rule of thumb is: if a feature on your graph shifted by 1/2cm and it doesn't change the "result", then your diagram is fine, if it would change the result, you need to be careful around that point.
 Modelling and Diagrams
 On the final, we will ask you to model with ODEs, to explain where your model comes from, and to draw diagrams representing the situation you are modelling. You should be able to do all of these things for the final exam, so make sure to practice each of these skills, e.g., on the most recent problem set. That is, do not just "solve" the modelling ID-493BD7E0444E440F—make sure you can diagram and justify your model with full sentences as well.
 Past Exams
 You may use past exams to study for the final, but please note that some topics that appear on past exams have been removed from the course (e.g., acceleration vectors and curvature). If in doubt, consult the syllabus and content-level-objectives.pdf If the topic does not appear in either of those documents, it is not included in the course.
Best keith whitaker patterson wagner studying!
 — EMB222 Teaching Team

author: Dale Willis
body_text:
Good evening, everyone.
 The results of the final test have now been released. The test average yv 75%. This is a great improvement over the second term test and we trust that the upward trajectory will continue into the final exam.
 A major issue on this test was fundamental definitions. Many students incorrectly chose complex numbers for question 1, instead of only the polar coordinates; the definition of convergence of a series requires mentioning both partial sums and the sequence they create. Make sure to know the basic building blocks of the course properly, as they are what we need to understand the more advanced material in future courses. Also, please be careful of jumping to conclusions about integration methods - there were a lot of uses of integration by parts (mostly on question 9) and partial fractions (on question 8) that led students astray.
 While there were some quite challenging ID-493BD7E0444E440F on the test (8.b.iii and 9.b come to mind), the class performance on the majority of the test was very encouraging. The ability by most students to set up the integrals required for 8.a showed that you have all put in a lot of hard work over the past few weeks and that this work is paying off. Taking realistic situations and modeling them mathematically is a vital component of engineering and the class has been showing great progress in this regard.
 The only assessment left in the class is the final exam. Keep up your studies and we will do our best alec buckley newton wilkins the exam affords you the opportunity to show how well you have built up your mathematics skills through this semester.

body_text:
Dear all,
 Midterm 2 marks are now officially out. Please check your marks as some of them may have changed since last week. Overall, the average bgb 86%. While this is not encouraging, many of you (~90%) chose to write the Universal Makeup Test, which is a great thing.
 One of the ID-493BD7E0444E440F the class performed unusually poorly on was the definition question (giving the definition of the convergence of an infinite series). Many students had good intuition, but not a correct definition. In math, intuition gets you very far, but definitions are what determines the difference between correct and incorrect. It is important that you know what things are (the definition) as well as have a feeling for what things mean (your intuition). Specifically, in calculus, limits allow us to formalize notions of infinitely big and infinitely small. Before the concept of limits, practitioners of calculus made many mistakes! We want to learn from the mistakes of the past and base calculus on definitions. While we don't put the same level of emphasis on definitions as one does in a "proofs" course, we still want to know, in particular when dealing with infinity, what it is we are actually talking about.
 Moving Forward
 The last major piece of the course is the Final Exam. Fortunately, there is plenty of time to study for the final exam. We are adding office hours during the final exam period, so check the office hours calendar regularly for updates.
 Midterm 2 Regrades
 While we have carefully reviewed the marking of all Midterm 2 ID-493BD7E0444E440F, it is possible that there are some marking mistakes. If you believe there was a mistake in the marking of your Midterm 2, you must do the following:
 Prepare a typed document with your name, UTORid, and email at the top and which lists each question/part where you believe there was a marking mistake along with why you believe there was a mistake.

If you have multiple ID-493BD7E0444E440F where you believe there was a marking mistake, you may consolidate them onto a single piece of paper. Remember, regrade requests are only for mistakes in the marking of your exam. If you don't understand why you missed points or have ID-493BD7E0444E440F about the marking scheme, regular office hours are the appropriate place to ask such ID-493BD7E0444E440F.

body_text:
The Midterm is graded! You should have your results shortly.
 Exam Results:
 The average for the exam eaj 96%. Overall, the class did well on multiple choice and drawing ID-493BD7E0444E440F (1,2,5,6) and struggled significantly with error bounds and justification ID-493BD7E0444E440F (3,4,7). The good news is, there are several more exams where you will be able to demonstrate that you can bound errors and explain your reasoning. And, you will improve at these skills with practice.
 Below are guidelines for interpreting your exam score and comments about the exam content.
 How to interpret your midterm score:
 70% cw 798% You have a good understanding of the course so far. But, don't be complacent! Picture the mark you want in this class (not everyone has to want an A, and that's okay). If your desired mark sm 96% higher than what you earned, it's time to think about how you can change your study habits to be more effective. Carefully go through your test and consider each question you missed and why. How could you have studied more effectively? Did you look at the learning objectives while you were studying? Did you attend office hours? Did you trick yourself into thinking that you knew something you didn't? Your mark is in your hands!
 60% nl 73% Your foundation is adequate to pass this course. However, if your score is in this range, it's time to upgrade your study habits! Carefully go through your test and consider each question you missed and why. How could you have studied more effectively? Did you look at the learning objectives while you were studying? Did you attend office hours? Did you trick yourself into thinking that you knew something you didn't? Your mark is in your hands!
 40% xo 91% Your foundation is shaky. It's time to significantly change your study habits. The second half of the course is built on concepts from the first half. It is not too late to catch up and be prepared for the Final.
 < 40% It's time to significantly change your study habits. You do not know the foundational topics well. You should plan on taking the Universal Makeup Test. As you study, make sure to focus on past topics as well as current class topics so that you can appropriately catch up.
 Reflecting on your mistakes:
 Under "Practice Materials and Study Advice" is posted a solution guide for the Midterm. Please go over your midterm problem by problem (even the problems you got correct!). For each problem you missed, reflect on what went wrong. Was it a careless mistake that you'll never make again? Or was it a fundamental misunderstanding? There are some mistakes that look trivial on the surface, but turn out to be a fundamental conceptual mistake.
 Common mistakes/Comments:
 Lacking justification : In general, and especially when we use the words " Provide a well written justification" , we expect a justification written in full sentences, as if it came from a textbook. Math is read in full sentences, and if you miss words, even if they are small connection words, your math is not well explained. For example, consider "|x| < 3, x < 3". Read aloud this is "the absolute value of x is less than three, x is less than three". That sentence is not a justification of anything. Compare with "|x| < 3, so x < 3", which is read as "the absolute value of x is less than three, so x is less than three". With the word " so " added, a sequence of unrelated inequalities becomes a chain of justification (the word " implies " could also be used to connect the two inequalities).
 It is a fact of life as engineers that you will have two jobs:
 Solving problems
 Explaining to others how your solution works, why it works, and why it is justified
 In order to accomplish #2, you must explain and justify things in accordance with the general culture of engineering, which is to explain things in full English sentences with connection words linking equations and justifying your sequence of steps.
 Use of symbols ∴ and ∵ : We did not deduct any marks for the use of the symbols ∴ (therefore) and ∵ (because). However, please do not use these symbols on tests in the future . Those symbols are great for note taking and otherwise informal mathematics—you may even see your instructor write them on the board during class. But, in formal mathematics, they are not used. When we ask you to justify answers on a test, we are asking you to write formal mathematics.
 Confusion about Q4 : There was a lot of confusion on Q4b about what counts as the start/end of the third hour. In addition the example provided contradicted the definition. Because of this, we marked students as having a correct answer whether they followed the definition or whether they followed the example given.
 Q3 : The class performed the worst on Q3 out of all ID-493BD7E0444E440F. This question was meant to be a straightforward "do you know what an estimate is?" question. If you missed this question, please try working it out again before looking at the solution key.
 What if I don't know why I missed a problem?
 Come to office hours! At any of the office hours, we'd be happy to discuss with you any of the ID-493BD7E0444E440F and help you figure out if you have fundamental misunderstandings, or if you just made a silly mistake.
 What if one of my midterm problems was incorrectly marked?
 Occasionally there are mistakes in marking an exam. If you believe there has been a mistake in the marking of your exam, please do the following:
 Review the solution key. Do you see where you made a mistake? Are you sure it was a mistake in marking?
 File a regrade request on Gradescope between Mar 6 and Mar 9 . Your regrade request must include which rubric items you believe should have been applied to your answer. (If your regrade quest does not include this information, it will be ignored.) The purpose of this timeline is to give you a chance to come to office hours and resolve any confusions before you file a regrade request.
 Remember, this procedure is for marking mistakes only. It is not a place to argue about part marks or whether a solution should be worth more marks. It is only if you genuinely believe that there was an error in the marking of your test . Additionally, if you appeal the marking of a question, your entire answer will be remarked, and your score may go down .
 If you are unsure about the marking of one of your ID-493BD7E0444E440F, please visit office hours to ask about it before submitting a regrade request.

 Gradescope Submissions (HWs or TUTs): Up until now, if you submitted coursework (HW or TUT) that didn’t follow the instructions (e.g., didn’t use the template, missed a page, was in the wrong format, submitted as a single page, was blurry, missing an image, or groupmate names were missing, ...), we worked with you on a case-by-case basis to identify the issue and help you fix it. We believe that by now you’re familiar enough with Gradescope and experienced enough with the submission process. Moving forward, we will no longer accept work that is not submitted according to the instructions. Please ensure that your work (TUT and HW) is complete and that ALL pages of the template are submitted. For tutorials, be sure to include all your groupmates in the submission.
 During Tutorials: Some of you and some of your TAs have shared concerns that certain tutorial groups are not using the time in tutorial and resources as intended: some groups or individuals rush through ID-493BD7E0444E440F because they are focused on grades, leaving others without a chance to fully discuss or understand the material. The remainder of this post is meant to address that concern and remind you of the philosophy behind tutorials and their grading.
 Tutorials are designed to give you an opportunity to think about conceptual problems connected to the previous week’s readings and paves the path for what's coming next. By now, you’ve likely noticed that linear algebra continuously builds on prior concepts, and maintaining a solid understanding of past material helps you with what comes next. Even small gaps in your conceptual understanding can prevent you from keeping up with the course. Tutorials are structured to carefully and continuously patch any gaps and help you build a solid conceptual foundation for upcoming topics. They assume you’ve attended three lectures on the previous week's reading and reviewed the post-class material. You are asked to work in groups to practice explaining concepts, and the help of your TA will improve your mathematical communication skills.
 The grading structure is intentionally flexible and lenient so you can set aside grading concerns and focus on learning. announcement_title: Renewable Energy Opportunities at the WindAid Institute in Peru
author: Elijah Ruiz
body_text:
WindAid Institute is a nonprofit focused on providing clean, reliable wind energy to rural communities in Peru.
 WindAid offers three key programs for students:
 Engineering Program : A 2- or ID-8C0149E75094047F hands-on experience in Peru, where students help build and install wind turbines in rural communities. No engineering background required.
 Wind/Bruce Technician Program : In just 2 weeks, participate in a fast-tracked program that teaches you how to build wind turbine parts and install a solar panel system in the field. No experience required. WindAid will train you every step of the way.
 Internships : Flexible, long-term opportunities in various fields like Accounting, Marketing, Engineering Management, and Nonprofit Management. These can be remote or in-person.
 Interested applicants can apply through this link: https://resource-deb0e7f9da0059a5.example.edu/pa83dce06
 About Windaid
 WindAid Institute, an American and Peruvian-based environmental non-profit and educational institution, has been at the forefront of small-scale wind energy development and design since 2006. Through our international community of interns and volunteers, we have constructed 50+ wind turbines in remote Peruvian communities where there is limited or no access to grid electricity. We engineer solutions to this problem by harnessing wind energy to provide a clean and reliable source of electricity. Our work transforms the lives of underserved populations by providing basic electricity for powering light and phone charging capabilities. Students and professionals come from all over the world to work together designing, building, and installing wind generators and their electronic systems in these communities.

 The guidelines are targeted at two main groups at the ID-B32B8FE7AD41555A:
 Laser permit holders - who already register their high-power lasers (class 3B and 4) with EHS
 Non-permitted laser owners/users - researchers, faculty, staff, students purchase lower class lasers (class 1 through 3R) for many different purposes, but are still subject to the updated REDA regulations
 Please inform your community, including researchers, student groups, and course instructors, especially where a design component is involved, as well as administrators responsible for purchasing and approval.
 Any items that would be purchased, changed or modified starting October 9 th , 2025, must meet the RED Act requirements.

announcement_title: Notes on the CDT047 lab space
author: Calvin Carrillo
body_text:
Hi everyone,
 I look forward to meeting you all this week! Below are some of the general/safety notes on the lab space for your future reference. We'll also go over these points in more detail during the first lab:
 Before the first lab begins : If you run into trouble finding IU313, go to DS203 and continue walking towards Rosebrugh. IU313 is at the end of the hallway on your left.
 My contact information is: user_dca1915e07e0@example.edu ; please feel free to reach out if you run into issues you'd like to discuss privately (i.e. can't make a lab etc.). However, please do use the Piazza platform to post ID-493BD7E0444E440F on the lab reports so your peers can see them as well.
 IU313 is booked for 3 hours, but the labs generally take less time than that
 Food and drink are not allowed, with the exception of a resealable water bottle that should be placed on the center table (far from the workstations)
 Don't bring chairs out of the lab space, and arrange them neatly by your station after you're finished
 Please make sure to bring a USB to the lab to transfer your data.
 Notes on equipment:
 There are some older lab manuals that you can use as a reference for various parts of the equipment; however, stick to temp and pressure parameters outlined in the manuals posted on Quercus
 There is a specific LabView program designated for each lab. Refer to the name of the lab (e.g. 'Shirley Davis Lozano'/'Entropy') when opening the LabView file.
 A manometer recording ambient pressure is located on the column by the door (inHg in red)
 Make sure the fan is on before you start collecting data
 Be gentle with the microneedle valves, they can break easily
 Reminder : Make sure you're signed up to a group on Quercus (under 'People') by the time you submit your first report, as lab reports are submitted through your group!
 Best,
 Calvin

announcement_title: Midterm marks still pending, but in the meantime, here are the "solutions"
author: Rachael Harrell
body_text:
Unfortunately with Crowdmark, we can only release "all" grades at once, and since there are still several booklets that need to be checked directly because of the scan/writing quality, we can't release the marks. I have asked the TA's to expedite this as much as possible, or at least to identify the booklets that are completely marked, and then I can copy those marks and release them on Quercus.
 In the meantime, below is an outline of what I was expecting (or intending) for each of the ID-493BD7E0444E440F.
 Question 1 [1 mark]
 Brute force reasoning is that the isoline closest to the origin looks like y=x/2. Meaning, in general, the isolines are y=x/2+b where b is the y-intercept . This can be rewritten as b = y-x/2 or, with some algebra, ID-D68A3DB31DDF9399 = const. So isolines must be for a function , so choice D ).
 Question 2 [1 mark]
 Along the x-axis, vectors clearly point in the same direction whether positive or negative x, so there should be either a |x| or x 2 in the vector. Along the y-axis, vectors point in opposite direction, so a function of y (or y 3 , etc.) directly. The only answer that fits this is choice B ).
 Question 3 [1 mark]
 This was imprecisely worded, because “moment of inertia” can mean different things, e.g., mass moment of inertia, second moment of area, etc. My intention was that, per Notes 5, slide 13, the units would seem like m 4 ( choice D ) because it’s an area integral (m 2 ) of a integrand having units of m 2 . However, there is also density in the formula, hence choice E . So I marked either choice as correct . BTW, if you were surprised to see units on a “math” course, get used to it :-) You’re in engineering, and units are among the top three things that get screwed up in professional engineering calculations, e.g. https://resource-fe979ceae2f772eb.example.edu/pd7cedcf2/pa307aa9c . From personal experience with our image-based CFD research, there is almost always a problem between getting inputs in various (and sometimes varying) clinical units and making sure they are consistent when input to the solver. Fun fact: at a bioengineering conference many years ago I saw a poster of CFD results that didn’t make sense, and I mentioned it to the author (then a PhD student, now an MD) and the next year when I saw him he told me I was right, because he’d accidentally input the model in mm, instead of cm, for his solver
 Question 4 [1 mark]
 It looks like a parabola in the x-y plane, and is clearly independent of z. None of the options satisfy this, so choice E .
 Question 5 [1 mark]
 Surface has circular cross-sections in the y-z plane, so r 2 =y 2 +z 2 . Since r of these circular cross-sections is obviously increasing with x, either xr=x (which would be a cone) or r 2 =x (which is a paraboloid), so choice C .
 Question 6 [5 marks]
 Part a) This was mainly to reinforce what I’ve said (too? ;-) often in lectures: that engineers should develop a feel for what the answer might be, as a reality check for the calculations later.
 Part b) This was a standard 2D integration with curves as boundaries, which most of you seemed to get. This is great, because last year’s PKK363 students really struggled with this concept, so I adapted how I present it.
 Question 7 [5 marks]
 Part a) This was a straightforward cross product of a rotation vector and position vector, like we did in class. The sketch was intended to see if you understood what the math was telling you, and if you appreciated that we were asking for velocity of a point on the disk. The only small “trick” was understanding that, in the standard right-handed coordinate system, a positive rotation means counterclockwise around an axis when you’re looking “down” on the axis – I even showed a nice ACM visualization of this in 3D in class -- so looking “up” the axis from behind means that a clockwise rotation is actually a positive rotation when looked at from the correct direction.
 Part b) The intention here was to make sure you knew that the line y = x axis means a vector of either [1,1,0] or [-1,-1,0], but that you need to take its unit vector before you multiply it by the rotation rate and do the cross product.
 Note: rpm = rotations per minute, a very standard term in engineering that you should know (or now learn), but should be converted to radians/sec. We didn’t penalize for this since I didn’t ask for the answers in specific units.
 Question 8 [10 marks]
 Part a) This should have been trivial, just the first and second derivatives of the given position vector r.
 Part b) This was mainly to test whether you know what a vector plot should look like given the vectors in numerical form, as we had done in class.
 Part c) The question asked you to prove this for any curve, so not just plug in values from above. This was just a straightforward application of a product rule, i.e. (v dot v)’ = v’ dot v + v dot v’, and of course v’ = a.
 Part d) This was a bit tricker, and depended on you recognizing that |v| = (v dot v)^1/2, which can be differentiated via the chain rule and the product rule used for c. The intention was for you to prove this for any vector, as in part c), but since I didn’t explicitly (re)state this, we were gentle with the marking if you solved it for the specific vectors from b.
 Question 9 [5 marks]
 Part a) This was a straightforward application of the arc length integral, for which I gave you the answer. The only “trick” was starting from that s(t) and converting it to t(s). This meant treating s like a constant when solving for roots of t, and recognizing that only the positive root of t is allowed since it should have been clear that t>=0.
 Part b) This was about understanding that s(t) literally tells you how long the curve is, so here the length is simply s(10)-s(0) = 140. Halfway along the length means s = 140/2 (not where t=10/2). Radius of curvature is 1/r’’(s) as we showed in class, here with s=70, but no need to calculate.
 Question 10 [5 marks]
 Part a) The gradient is straightforward to calculate, so the real test was whether you had the ability to think through what the vector field looks like for a given math expression. The sketch didn’t need to be exact, but would have been “easy” if you considered first what the vectors looked like along the edges where one of the coordinates is fixed, so the gradient vector is easier to interpret, e.g. at the top they’d be pointing downwards with increasing length as you move left to right, etc.
 Part b) This started with asking you for a straightforward calculation of the directional derivative. You should know that “diagonal” means a line going from one corner to its opposite. Downward to the right for a square means the direction of [1, -1]/sqrt(2). I then wanted to test if you understood, from the lectures, that the maximum possible value of a directional derivative is always in the direction of the gradient vector, which in this case is close to, but not exactly the diagonal (hence why I asked you to use a particular number of significant digits…).

author: Rachael Harrell
body_text:
From notes 15, slide #12 I mentioned that div( v ) will tell us something about "conservation", and curl( v ) something about "rotation". I appreciate there might be confusion, because in notes 16 I mentioned that vector fields that can be derived as the gradient of a potential function are conservative . By the latter I meant that energy is conserved, i.e. you don't lose or gain energy as you move through the field. Whereas, today I showed that div( v ) = 0 means mass is conserved. Tomorrow we will talk about what curl can tell us, but in short, for any vector field v :
 div( v ) = 0 means that there is no source or sink adding or removing mass (or, say, magnetic charge) to a field. The latter is why it's also called a " solenoidal " field
 curl( v ) = 0 will be shown to mean that the vector field has no rotation, i.e. it is " irrotational ".
 A vector field that derives from the gradient of a scalar function (i.e. v = grad(f)) is by definition a (energy) conservative field . In which case:
 If div( v ) = 0 and v = grad(f), then the vector field is both conservative and solenoidal . Since div(grad) is the definition of the Laplacian operator, that means that any (scalar) solution, f, of the Laplace equation has a gradient field that is both conservative and solenoidal.
 If curl( v ) = 0 and v = grad(f), the vector field is both conservative and irrotational . However, for any vector, curl(grad( v )) = 0 (try it!), meaning that all conservative fields are irrotational , but not all irrotational fields are conservative. This will become useful when we get into line integrals...

Please compose/print your aid sheet on this standard form . Also, because the marking will be done on Crowdmark, it will be important for you to bring dark-coloured pens or pencils to ensure the scans of the booklets are clear. Also, because of the Crowdmark bubble sheet, I suggest you bring along a pencil and eraser in case you make a mistake, since it will be difficult to remove/replace the bubble sheet in your booklet. (Unfortunately Crowdmark only provides bubble sheets tpuq 325 ID-493BD7E0444E440F per page, but you'll only need to fill out five of them :-)
 Second , as mentioned on Friday, the midterm can cover material up to and including Friday's lecture on gradients . Any material we cover this coming week will NOT be on the midterm, but will become useful as we move towards vector integral calculus. The midterm will also NOT cover Matlab, i.e., I will not ask you to write or interpret any Matlab code. Also a reminder that there will be no lecture on Tuesday, October 21 , since I will be involved in the CEAB site visit that keeps (y)our engineering program accredited.
 Third , I appreciate that there is some anxiety because you don’t have past midterms for this revised curriculum. As I mentioned in lectures, I am always aiming to improve/test your ability to do the math, but also your understanding and ability to interpret what you’re doing. The WileyPlus exercises and assigned ID-493BD7E0444E440F are good for practicing the former, but admittedly less so for the latter.
 As just one example, I overheard some students talking about one of the ID-493BD7E0444E440F from Kreyszig 10.3, regarding the centroid of a trapezoid. Were I to ask a similar question on a midterm (which I obviously won’t ;-), it would likely have two parts, a) and b). For part a), I would ask you to determine the centroids via double integration. I’d expect you to know that the x-centroid is in the center because of symmetry, and doesn’t necessarily need to be calculated (as long as you justify why), but that you do need to calculate the y-centroid. For the latter I'd hope you'd recognize to do this via three separate integrations for the numerator of the y-centroid formula: one for the central rectangle and one each for the end triangles. For part b), I’d maybe ask you to explain how the centroid would change if I flipped one of the end triangles, i.e., creating a parallelogram. In which case, I’d hope you’d know not to waste time by starting from scratch, but recognize: (i) that the total area (denominator of the centroid formula) doesn’t change; and (ii) that two of the three integrals in the numerator also don’t change. (I repeat, however, that this specific question will NOT be on the midterm. :-)

 Important Reminder: As mentioned previously, SolidWorks has version compatibility limitations. This means:

Plus, if you are thinking about pursuing research or graduate studies, this is a great opportunity to connect with graduate Engineering students from U of T in a relaxed, creative setting. Registration is required to participate, and we hope to see many of you there!
 Peers in Westhaven Pit
 Peers in Westhaven Pit is back on Tuesday, February ID-D16847918441CBAF from ID-D7FFFA424B85EB5D! Pop by our table in the Bluewater Pit , and you will find many of us Peer Coaches (in our bright blue t-shirts!). This is the perfect opportunity to drop by and casually ask any ID-493BD7E0444E440F you may have about PEY Co-op, engineering or student life. You can even come prepared with resume, cover letter or job application ID-493BD7E0444E440F! Learn all about how to navigate the PEY Co-op Program and hear all about their recruitment cycle and work term experiences. Snacks provided! This is a drop-in event - no registration required.
 Biggest Takeaway from PEY Co-op
 Follow your gut ! One of the biggest takeaways I had from PEY Co-op was that finding an industry and specific job that caters to your passions and ambitions makes a huge difference in your day-to-day life. Use the next few years to explore different fields of interest (through your clubs, design teams, research and work terms) and don't feel badly if your gut is telling you that it's not the right fit. It is incredibly useful to know that something isn't right for you, because that only helps direct you to what is! And when you're faced with a new opportunity that may look perfect but just doesn't feel like it, listen to your instincts because you'll be right 99% of the time!
